description: We are a Greece–Lithuania team creating EARTH WITHOUT EYES: an accessible instrument that turns NASA Earth visualization frames into explorable sound. Our prototype includes keyboard-controlled spatial listening, transparent image-to-audio mappings, and blind A/B comparisons. We combine software, mathematical reasoning, Earth science and audio design. We welcome accessibility testing and rigorous scientific feedback. Live prototype: https://earth-without-eyes-2026.vercel.app/
summary:
What if you could interrogate a NASA image with your ears?
Earth Without Eyes is a browser-based scientific listening instrument that turns selected visible features in three NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into real-time, inspectable sound. Rather than composing background music inspired by Earth, we analyze the rendered image itself: documented color classifiers produce a 96-position signal, and explicit rules translate feature density and visual position into audible patterns. Visitors can trace what they hear back to the image, isolate and examine a sound, compare two regions without seeing them, and download evidence that makes the computations open to scrutiny.
Our three listening worlds are ISS lightning, Black Marble changes in night lights, and GEDI forest structure. The interface combines a visual Observatory with an ear-first challenge and a reproducible evidence trail. Its distinguishing principle is simple: a beautiful sound is not enough; it should be explainable, falsifiable, and open to question.
This is an exploratory multisensory interpretation of NASA-authored visualizations—not calibrated geophysical-data sonification, a verified assistive technology, or a claim of NASA endorsement. We hope to make scientific imagery more approachable while giving scientists and listeners a transparent way to question how an image becomes sound.
details:
The NASA Earth Information Center communicates major planetary stories through sophisticated imagery. But a visually compelling graphic is not automatically explorable through hearing. We built Earth Without Eyes as an experiment in an alternative kind of scientific access: instead of writing music about Earth, we give NASA-authored visual frames a specific, inspectable acoustic representation.

Three genuine NASA stories. Users can choose ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor detections, NASA Black Marble night-light change graphics, or a GEDI forest-height visualization. The project explicitly distinguishes the authentic NASA frames inside the instrument from decorative concept artwork on its landing page. The app preserves image aspect ratio, names its source, and does not silently substitute fabricated NASA data when an upstream asset is unavailable.

Live, rule-based sonification. The browser samples predefined regions of each rendered frame and applies source-specific RGB feature masks. Its horizontal scan has 96 signal positions. The proportion of pixels matching an image-specific visual feature contributes to audible density/intensity; their vertical image distribution contributes to pitch; horizontal position can contribute to stereo pan. Sounds are generated using the Web Audio API when the user requests playback. An image-synchronized signature and documented rules expose how these visual features lead to sound. These are properties of rendered graphics, not direct measurements of lightning frequency, calibrated radiance, or physical canopy height.

A challenge you cannot solve by looking. In our Blind Earth Discovery and comparative listening experiences, users hear two selected regions and decide which carries more of the chosen color-coded visual signal. In research mode, the image and visual cues are hidden, pitch and panning cues are standardized for the comparison, and answer feedback is delayed. This yields an interactive, falsifiable task rather than a claim that music universally communicates scientific information.

An auditable evidence trail. Local JSON exports record source provenance, feature measurements and computed outputs. A separate verifier can recompute the image-derived counts and check selected receipts and note schedules against explicit rules, including detection of deliberately corrupted records. This establishes numerical reproducibility within the implemented pipeline; it does not authenticate NASA servers, prove physical-data calibration, or certify what a listener heard through a particular device.

Why it matters. A scientific visualization can invite curiosity but obscure how its visual encoding becomes an interpretation. We designed the interface around transparency: users may listen, inspect, test, and challenge the mapping. The conceptual goal is a more accountable pathway toward multisensory Earth science, useful for education and for future accessibility research. We do not claim that we have achieved clinically validated assistive access.

Technical implementation. Browser-based HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Canvas-based inspection of NASA-authored raster visualization frames; Web Audio API oscillator synthesis; a small Vercel-hosted serverless proxy for retrieving the selected NASA media; optional user-uploaded images identified as unverified; local JSON export and independent checks. We tested the core processing with synthetic fixtures, intentionally corrupted test receipts and responsive-layout checks; those tests are not a substitute for a controlled human usability study or a full screen-reader audit.

Scientific limitations and next steps. Source graphic colors and compressed imagery can incorporate projections, legends and rendering decisions; matched-pixel fractions cannot be treated as physical observations. A mean vertical location can fall between separated clusters of matching pixels and fail to represent any individual feature; a future cluster-aware auditory mapping should preserve this ambiguity. Other next steps are to sonify underlying numerical NASA data products, conduct representative blind/low-vision user studies and broaden source and device validation.
dataRefs: ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS), NASA SVS #5011 — “Lightning Events Detected from the International Space Station (ISS) 2017–2023.” NASA's SVS imagery depicts quality-controlled lightning detections collected by LIS from January 2017 to July 2023 using a 10-day roving window. Our prototype sonifies selected plotted pixel/color features in an SVS preview frame, not lightning-rate counts or the source time series.

Black Marble Night Lights, NASA SVS #5313 — “Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023 – EIC Version.” Based on VIIRS/Black Marble imagery, this visualization uses purple for areas with more visible night-light signal and orange for areas with less during the comparison. Our application classifies rendered purple/orange features to produce audible contrasts and a blind comparison; the color-pixel fractions are not physical radiance-change units.

GEDI Forest Height, NASA SVS #4950 — “GEDI Forest Height.” Depicts GEDI lidar-derived canopy-height visualization, including data collected 2019–2020. Our prototype sonifies selected visible color/structure features; it does not claim to recover height measurements from pixel colors.
